This is a purely CONFIGURATION change in X-Ray (via console or PutSamplingRule), without the need to change code.
dva-avc-178.hint: Remember that X-Ray evaluates multiple sampling rules in order of priority, and each rule can have its own matching condition and fixed rate.
optionRationales: Right. X-Ray evaluates the Sampling Rules in order of PRIORIDADE (smaller numbers are evaluated first); the first rule whose condition (including response attributes) HTTP) matching the request is applied. Creating a high priority rule that houses with answers 5xx and has FixedRate=1.0, ensures that TODO error 5xx is sampled (full track), while the general rule with FixedRate=0.01 reduces the sampling of normal traffic to 1%. This is a purely CONFIGURATION change in X-Ray (via console or PutSamplingRule), without the need to change code.

Incorrect — the programmatic definition embedded in the code directly violates the requirement 'without changing the application code'. Furthermore, managing the sampling rate via Sampling Rules centralized in X-Ray is the recommended practice, as it allows to adjust the sampling behavior without need of re-deployment of the function.

Incorrect. Disable Active Tracing eliminates TODA Distributed tracking capacity — not only reduces volume, but completely removes the visibility needed to debug errors 5xx via X-Ray, which goes directly against the requirement to ensure that errors 5xx are always tracked with full trace.

Incorrect. The Reservoir Size defines a fixed number of tracks sampled per second before applying the fixedrate percentage over additional requests — it is not the only parameter that controls the fee. 5% would still result in approximately 5% additional traffic sampling (much above the target of 1%), and this approach does not create any mechanism to guarantee 100% error tracking 5xx.

dva-avc-179.text: An application is composed of the chain: Amazon API Gateway → AWS Lambda (OrderService) → Amazon DynamoDB, and the OrderService also invokes a second function, AWS Lambda (InventoryService), which in turn makes a call HTTP for a third party payment gateway. Users report that checkout requests are slow (average of 4 second), but it is not clear which chain component is responsible for most of this latency. The team wants to identify VISUALMENTE, in an aggregate way between many tracks (without inspecting individual track timelines one by one), which call/component contributes more to total latency. Active tracking is already enabled in both functions Lambda. Which feature of X-Ray meets this need?
options: Enable CloudWatch Contributor Insights in the Duration metric of each function Lambda, to identify which function has the highest value of P99 duration.

Open CloudWatch Logs for each of the two functions Lambda individually and manually correlate the log timestamps between the log groups for a sample of recent requests, estimating which function took longer.

Open the X-Ray Service Map, which displays all the services/us involved in tracking requests as a graph, showing the average latency of each node and visually highlighting the nodes with higher latency or error rate.
Add custom metrics via PutMetricData at the beginning and end of each function/call, and build a dashboard from CloudWatch to visually compare the durations.
dva-avc-179.explanation: Right. X-Ray's Service Map adds data from TODOS the corresponding traces in a visual graph, where each node represents a service/resource (including calls) HTTP external, such as third party payment gateway) and displays aggregate metrics such as average latency and error/fault rate. We with high latency appear prominent (usually in shades of yellow/red), allowing immediate and visual identification, without manual inspection of individual tracks, that the call to third party payment gateway is responsible for most of the 4 latency seconds.
dva-avc-179.hint: Think about which X-Ray display automatically aggregates the latency of all nodes of a call chain — including calls to external services — into a single graph.
optionRationales: Right. X-Ray's Service Map adds data from TODOS the corresponding traces in a visual graph, where each node represents a service/resource (including calls) HTTP external, such as third party payment gateway) and displays aggregate metrics such as average latency and error/fault rate. We with high latency appear prominent (usually in shades of yellow/red), allowing immediate and visual identification, without manual inspection of individual tracks, that the call to third party payment gateway is responsible for most of the 4 latency seconds.

Incorrect. Correlate manually timestamps between multiple log groups, for many requests, is extremely laborious and prone to errors — exactly the type of manual analysis the question asks to avoid. X-Ray's Service Map automatically performs this aggregation for all corresponding tracks.

Incorrect. The Contributor Insights identifies the main contributors (top-N) to a metric within a single resource/log, but does not provide an end-to-end view of the call chain between multiple services — and, crucially, would not capture the latency of the call HTTP to third party payment gateway, which is not a function Lambda with own Duration metric in CloudWatch. X-Ray's Service Map precisely covers this point-to-point view, including X-Ray-instrumented external calls SDK.

Incorrect. This approach requires significant code changes (called PutMetricData at each instrumentation point) and manual construction of a dashboard — considerable work to obtain something that the X-Ray Service Map already offers automatically, in an aggregate and visual way, since Active Tracing is enabled, without additional instrumentation for this basic latency view.

dva-avc-180.text: A team wants to enable distributed tracing to a function AWS Lambda, so that its execution — and the calls it makes to downstream services from AWS way SDK, as Amazon DynamoDB — appear automatically in the AWS X-Ray, SEM need to manually instrument each call from SDK in the code. The function already uses the AWS X-Ray SDK to encapsulate the client's AWS SDK (for example, via AWSXRay.captureAWS(AWS) in Node.js). What configuration is required in the function Lambda to enable this?
options: Enable tracking mode ACTIVE in the function configuration Lambda (for example, Tracing: Active in a template SAM, or TrackingConfig.Mode = Active via CloudFormation/API).
In the handler code, create and manually start a new X-Ray segment with new AWSXRay.Segment(...), calling .close() at the end of the run, without enabling the tracking in the function configuration.
Implant X-Ray daemon in an instance EC2 separate, acting as sidecar, and configure to VPC Function config Lambda to send the tracking data to this instance EC2.
Configure function tracking mode Lambda as PASSTHROUGH.
dva-avc-180.explanation: Correct. Active mode automatically allows the execution roll of the function to the necessary X-ray permissions (xray:PutTraceSegments, xray:PutTelemetryRecords) and makes the running environment managed from Lambda run the X-Ray daemon and automatically manage the main segment for each invocation. Combined with X-Ray SDK encapsulating the client AWS SDK (captureAWS), each call to a downstream service, such as DynamoDB GetItItem, automatically generates a subsegment — no need for additional manual instrumentation of each call.
dva-avc-180.hint: Consider which function tracking configuration Lambda it is necessary for it itself to participate in the sampling and generate segments automatically, instead of just passing decisions from another service.
optionRationales: Correct. Active mode automatically allows the execution roll of the function to the necessary X-ray permissions (xray:PutTraceSegments, xray:PutTelemetryRecords) and makes the running environment managed from Lambda run the X-Ray daemon and automatically manage the main segment for each invocation. Combined with X-Ray SDK encapsulating the client AWS SDK (captureAWS), each call to a downstream service, such as DynamoDB GetItItem, automatically generates a subsegment — no need for additional manual instrumentation of each call.

Incorrect. The PassThrough mode only passes the tracking header (X-Amzn-Trace-Id) if the invocation service (e.g., API Gateway) has already taken the sampling decision and enabled tracking — the function Lambda in itself does not actively generate its own segments/subsegments of tracking in this mode. The Active mode is necessary for the function itself Lambda actively participates in sampling and segment generation.

Incorrect. Managing segments manually in the code is unnecessary and, without the Active enabled mode in the function configuration, incomplete — execution roll may not have the necessary X-Ray permissions and the X-Ray daemon may not be available in the running environment. Enable Active Tracing automatically treats daemon, permissions and creation of the main segment.

Incorrect. By enabling Active Tracing in a function Lambda, the managed execution environment already runs the X-Ray daemon automatically as part of the infrastructure of the X-Ray daemon. Lambda — there is no need or official support to implement and manage a separate X-ray daemon in an instance EC2 for this purpose.
